name: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
info: A coalition led by the Roman general Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I fought the Huns and their vassals under Attila in Gaul in 451 CE; Theodoric was killed, Attila withdrew, and the outcome is disputed.

facts.date: 20 June 451 CE, a date first proposed by J. B. Bury and accepted by many; some authors have proposed the first week of July or 27 September, and Hydatius's chronicle secures the battle to June
facts.place: Somewhere on the Catalaunian Plains in Gaul, near Châlons-en-Champagne or Troyes in present-day France; the site is disputed, and the ridge at Montgueux, west of Troyes, is the most thoroughly researched proposal
facts.sides: A coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Alans and other allies under the general Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I, against the Huns and their vassals under King Attila; no reliable strengths survive, and modern estimates for the allied Germanic forces run under 50,000 and for Attila's army closer to 70,000
facts.outcome: Theodoric was killed and both sides suffered heavy losses. Attila withdrew from Gaul; whether the battle was a Roman and allied victory or an indecisive one is disputed.

t: The sources give casualties of 165,000 (Jordanes) and almost 300,000 (Hydatius), figures that are implausibly high, though all the primary sources record the battle as exceptionally bloody.
Many historians (Bury, Hughes, Bachrach, Kim) hold that the siege of Aurelianum, not the battle, was the turning point of the campaign, since the battle was fought as Attila was already leaving Gaul.
Contemporary sources describe the battle as inconclusive and credit Aetius; later writers made it a Gothic victory and a point of Gothic pride.
dyk: The exact site of the battle is still unknown: scholars place it near Châlons-en-Champagne or Troyes, and a rich burial found at Pouan-les-Vallées in 1842, first thought to be Theodoric's, has not been shown to be related to the battle.
ev: The King of the Franks dies and his two sons dispute the succession, the elder seeking Attila's help and the younger siding with Aetius
Honoria sends a ring and a request for help to Attila, who claims half the empire as a dowry
Attila crosses the Rhine and sacks Divodurum (Metz) on 7 April
Attila's final assault on Aurelianum on 14 June is broken off as the Roman coalition approaches
The two armies meet on the Catalaunian Plains, about 20 June, and Theodoric is killed
Thorismund returns to Tolosa and becomes king of the Visigoths, while Attila leaves Gaul
Attila invades Italy, razes Aquileia and ravages the Po Valley before withdrawing

sections.background:
By 450 the Romans had restored their authority in much of Gaul, although control over the provinces beyond Italy was continuing to diminish. Armorica was only nominally imperial, and Germanic peoples on Roman land were bound by treaty as foederati under their own leaders. The Visigoths on the Garonne were restive but held to their treaty, the Burgundians awaited an opening for revolt, and the Alans on the Loire, loyal since 411, were more dependable.

The sources give different reasons for Attila's invasion. Jordanes states that the Vandal king Genseric enticed him to attack the Visigoths, but Jordanes's account of Gothic history is notoriously unreliable, and modern scholars think the explanation projects later events onto Attila's time. Other contemporary writers point to Justa Grata Honoria, sister of the emperor Valentinian III, who in 450 sent the eunuch Hyacinthus to Attila asking for help in escaping her confinement. Allegedly Attila took this as an offer of marriage and claimed half the empire as a dowry; Valentinian refused. Ian Hughes suggests she was using Attila's status as honorary magister militum as political leverage. A Frankish succession dispute added to it: the elder son of the dead king sought Attila's help, and the younger sided with Aetius, who adopted him.

Attila crossed the Rhine early in 451 and sacked Metz on 7 April, which Schultheis thinks may be a literary trope. By June he had reached Aurelianum (Orléans), whose people shut their gates, and he besieged it. His final assault on 14 June was broken off because the Roman coalition was approaching.
sections.forces:
Both armies were made up of many peoples. Besides the Romans, Alans and Visigoths, Jordanes lists Aetius's allies as the Francii, Sarmatae, Armoriciani, Liticiani, Burgundiones, Saxones, Riparii and Olibrones, together with other Celtic and German tribes. Peter Heather suggests that the Visigoths may have fielded about 25,000 men. Schultheis argues that the Germanic federates could on paper number more than 70,000 but probably numbered under 50,000, and that the Roman field army at the time of the battle was approximately 20,500 comitatenses and 18,000 limitanei. A. H. M. Jones's study of the Notitia Dignitatum gives just under 46,000 for units in Gaul in 395 to 425, an estimate that changes with new research.

Jordanes lists the Gepids under Ardaric and Gothic groups led by the Amali brothers Valamir, Theodemir and Videmir among Attila's allies. Sidonius Apollinaris gives a longer list, but E. A. Thompson suspects that some names come from literary tradition, since several peoples had disappeared centuries earlier. Thompson doubted that Attila could have fed even 30,000, and Lindner argues that the Great Hungarian Plain could support only 15,000 mounted nomads. Schultheis finds that the sources add up to more than 100,000 on paper but probably about 70,000.

On Jordanes's account the Visigoths held the right, the Romans the left, and Sangiban's Alans, of uncertain loyalty, the middle. Hughes argues that the Huns stood in the centre with their vassals on the wings, and that Aetius put the Alans in the middle because they were skilled cavalry who could fight beside Roman troops.
sections.course:
On learning of the invasion, Aetius moved his army from Italy to Gaul. Sidonius Apollinaris says he led few and scattered auxiliaries, which probably reflects that most of his army was already in Gaul and Sidonius's wish to favour Avitus. Aetius first tried to bring in Theodoric, who allegedly preferred to wait and fight the Huns on his own land, and then turned to Avitus, who according to tradition persuaded Theodoric and other wavering peoples. The coalition assembled at Arles and Toulouse and reached Aurelianum on 14 June. It then pursued Attila, who was leaving Gaul. The night before the main battle, Jordanes reports, allied Franks skirmished with Gepids loyal to Attila, with 15,000 dead on each side, a figure that cannot be verified.

By tradition Attila's diviners foretold disaster for the Huns and the death of one enemy leader, and he delayed until the ninth hour, about 2:30 pm. Hughes thinks the divination may be a fabrication and that both sides simply spent the day deploying. According to Jordanes, the Huns seized the right of a ridge and the Romans the left, and the Romans under Aetius and the Goths under Thorismund won the crest. Theodoric was killed in the assault without his men noticing, thrown from his horse and trampled or slain by the spear of the Amali Andag. The Visigoths fell on Attila's household unit and he took refuge in his wagon-fortified camp. Thorismund, returning in the dark, wandered into the camp and was wounded, and Aetius spent the night with the Goths.
sections.aftermath:
The next day the field was piled with bodies and the Huns did not come out. The allies began to besiege Attila's camp, and Jordanes says Attila built a funeral pyre of saddles to throw himself on if it was attacked. The Visigoths found Theodoric's body where the dead lay thickest and bore him away with songs in sight of the enemy. Thorismund wanted to storm the camp, but Aetius dissuaded him, fearing, says Jordanes, that if the Huns were wholly destroyed the Visigoths would leave their allegiance to Rome. Thorismund returned to Toulouse and became king without resistance. Gregory of Tours claims that Aetius dismissed his Frankish allies in the same way and kept the booty. Hughes thinks it likely that Aetius did advise them to go, as the Franks were fighting a civil war and Thorismund had five brothers.

Hydatius says almost 300,000 men are said to have fallen, and Jordanes gives 165,000 dead, not counting the earlier skirmish. These figures are implausibly high. Attila returned in 452 and invaded Italy. After a siege of three months, which Aetius had hoped would use up the campaigning season, he razed Aquileia and ravaged the Po Valley. Aetius had no help from the federates in Gaul and sent Pope Leo I, Trygetius and Gennadius Avienus to negotiate. Attila withdrew, most likely because of famine and disease in his army, and died in 453.
sections.sources:
The primary sources say little about the outcome apart from Jordanes, and all stress the casualties. Hydatius, who lived at the time, places the battle between the appearance and disappearance of Halley's Comet and says the Huns were defeated with the aid of God. Prosper, a contemporary, says the slaughter was incalculable and that the Huns appear to have been defeated because the survivors lost their taste for fighting. The Gallic Chronicle of 452 says that Attila inflicted and suffered defeat and then withdrew, and the chronicle of 511 names Tricasses, the Mauriac plain, and Theodoric's death by an uncertain hand. From the early sixth century, beginning with Cassiodorus, the battle came to be seen as an allied victory.

The account of Jordanes, who served as notary to Andag's son Gunthigis, is the fullest and is distorted. Hyun Jin Kim argues that it copies the Battle of Marathon, and Franz Altheim saw a fabrication modelled on Salamis. Kim's view that Attila won has received a mixed reception and is treated with scepticism. Schultheis argues that Jordanes reworked a narrative first written by the Goth Ablabius in 471 and expanded by Cassiodorus, and that heavy losses in the retreats led to an indecisive outcome that was later embellished into a Gothic victory.

The site is unresolved. The consensus is only that it lay near Châlons-en-Champagne or Troyes. Hodgkin proposed Méry-sur-Seine, Richardot La Cheppe and, in 2015, MacDowall the ridge at Montgueux, drawing on the Additamenta to Prosper, which place the battle five Roman miles from Troyes.
sections.legacy:
Opinion on the battle's importance divides. Edward Gibbon called it the last victory achieved in the name of the Western Roman Empire. Edward Creasy called it a triumph of Christian Europe over pagan savages of Asia, and John Julius Norwich wrote that the fate of western civilisation hung in the balance in 451 and 452. Modern authors have mostly moved away from this view. Geoffrey Parker called it a triumph of Roman defensive strategy, and Arther Ferrill notes that no single nation dominated either side and that two alliances fought in surprising coordination for the time. Meghan McEvoy sees Aetius's use of the federates as evidence of his diplomatic and administrative skills.

J. B. Bury held that its significance has been enormously exaggerated, that the campaign had been decided by cutting Attila off from Orléans, and that its value lay in damaging his prestige and weakening his forces. Hughes, Bachrach and Kim agree that the defence of Orléans was the real turning point. Bury and many others think the Battle of Nedao in 454 was more consequential for Europe, since the Hunnic hegemony disintegrated after it.

For Gaul, Hughes argues that the Goths came to believe they had not been adequately rewarded and later destroyed the Alans and besieged Orléans. Kim argues that the battle weakened the Alans, Visigoths and Romans and allowed Frankish and Burgundian hegemony in northern Gaul. Tackholm notes that later sources made the battle a point of Gothic pride, while Roman sources such as Procopius keep Aetius as the central figure.

summary: On about 20 June 451 a coalition of Romans, Visigoths and Alans under Aetius and Theodoric I fought Attila's Huns and their vassals in Gaul. Theodoric was killed and Attila left Gaul, but the site, the casualties and the battle's importance are all disputed.
references: Evan Schultheis, The Battle of the Catalaunian Fields, AD 451: Flavius Aetius, Attila the Hun, and the Transformation of Gaul (Pen & Sword Books Ltd., 2019)
Simon MacDowall, Catalaunian Fields AD 451, Rome's Last Great Battle (Osprey Publishing Ltd, 2015)
Ian Hughes, Aetius: Attila's Nemesis (Pen and Sword Books Ltd., 2012)
Hyun Jin Kim, The Huns, Rome, and the Birth of Europe (Cambridge University Press, 2013)
Iaroslav Lebedynsky, La campagne d'Attila en Gaule 451 apr. J.-C. (Lemme Edit, 2011)
Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire: A New History of Rome and the Barbarians (Oxford University Press, 2007)
notes: Outcome is disputed: the article sets out a Roman victory reading, an indecisive reading (Schultheis) and a Hunnic victory reading (Kim, treated with scepticism). I have not chosen one.
The site is unknown; the article names Montgueux as the most thoroughly researched proposal.
Dates: 20 June 451 is Bury's proposal; the article also mentions first week of July and 27 September. Metz on 7 April may be a literary trope (Schultheis).

Casualty figures (Hydatius 300,000, Jordanes 165,000, 15,000 each in the skirmish, Fredegar's Loire battle) are all called implausible or unverifiable. The article gives no reliable strengths; estimates for each side are scattered and inconsistent (Schultheis, Heather, Thompson, Lindner, Jones).
Jordanes's narrative is held to be distorted and partisan; Theodoric's death has two versions (trampled or slain by Andag).
The article contradicts itself slightly: it says the Huns pursued 'a plain with a hill' but modern scholars agree on a long ridge; Hughes's and MacDowall's placements of Thorismund differ.

Left out: the Franks' possible founder identities, Armorica details, the Treasure of Pouan's finer detail, Sidonius's full ally list, the sources' long quotations, Creasy's and Ferrill's block quotes.
The article's sentence on Fredegar says a prior battle on the Loire; not used.
